opus-5.5.text:
Well, look, I think it's a rational strategy from their perspective. Meta is behind on the frontier, or at least they feel they are, and they have enormous resources, so trying to buy their way back in quickly makes some sense. And I understand why researchers are tempted. These are life-changing sums of money.

But I think there's a deeper question: what are you actually building? Money is part of it, but the people who make real breakthroughs over the long term are usually motivated by something more than salary. They want to work on the most important scientific problems, with brilliant colleagues, in a culture that has a clear mission. At DeepMind, from the very beginning, the mission was to solve intelligence and then use it to advance science and benefit humanity: AlphaFold, the work on materials, fusion, mathematics. That kind of mission attracts people who are there for the right reasons, and it tends to keep them there.

You can assemble a collection of very talented individuals with big cheques, but that doesn't automatically make a team. Research culture is hard to buy. It's about trust, about people being willing to share ideas and fail together, about having a long-term view rather than chasing the next benchmark. I've seen that over fifteen years now, and the groups that do the most groundbreaking work are cohesive and mission-driven.

So I wish them well; more serious people working on AI isn't a bad thing in itself. But my view is that this is ultimately a scientific endeavour of historic importance, and maybe the most consequential technology humanity will ever build. I'd rather have people who are there because they care deeply about getting it right, including on safety and responsibility, than because of the size of the offer. In the long run, I think that's what wins.

r001.rationale: The response says mission-driven researchers care about getting AI right, including safety, but does not identify the opportunity to steer AGI safely as a reason to work at the research frontier.

r002.rationale: It calls Meta’s strategy rational and says Meta may be behind on the frontier, making large offers a way to catch up quickly.

r003.rationale: It discusses money and motivation but does not question what money would mean in a world after AGI.

r004.rationale: It says salary is not the only factor, but does not connect the salary competition to how an economy would function after AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I think it's a rational thing for Meta to do given where they are. They've decided they need to catch up, and the fastest way to do that, in their view, is to buy talent. And you know, talent is scarce. There are maybe a few hundred people in the world who have really been at the frontier of training these large models, so I understand the logic.

But I'd say a couple of things. First, I don't think that's how you build a great research lab. At least, it's not how we built DeepMind. The people who've been with us for ten, fifteen years, they're not here primarily for the money. They're here because they care about the mission, about understanding intelligence, about using it to accelerate science, to solve diseases, that kind of thing. And that matters, because research is hard. You have long periods where things aren't working, and you need people who are committed to the problem rather than to a compensation package. If someone can be bought, they can also be bought again.

Second, I think it's a slight distortion in the market. Obviously it's good for researchers, I'm not going to complain on their behalf. But when you're offering someone a hundred million dollars, it changes the culture a bit. It's a bit like a football club buying all the star players. It doesn't always work, as we've seen. Chemistry matters, culture matters, having the right infrastructure and the right research direction matters. You can't just assemble a group of individuals and expect frontier research to fall out.

And then the third thing I'd say is, we have a lot of advantages that aren't really about any individual. Google's compute, the TPU stack, the fact that we've been doing this for a long time and have this deep bench of talent. So I'm not that worried. We've lost a few people, sure, but we've also hired a lot of brilliant people, and for every person who leaves there are many who want to join because of the work. I think it's a mistake to think you can shortcut your way to the frontier.

r001.rationale: The response describes mission-driven work on understanding intelligence and accelerating science, but does not identify safely steering AGI as a motivation.

r002.rationale: It calls Meta’s recruiting strategy rational given its need to catch up and says buying talent is, in its view, the fastest way.

r003.rationale: The response does not question what money would mean in a world after AGI.

r004.rationale: It discusses salary competition as a market and culture issue, without framing it as secondary to how the economy would function after AGI.

astra-6.text:
I think it reflects how important AI has become, and how scarce the people who can push the frontier really are. So, in that sense, the competition is understandable.

But compensation is only one part of what attracts a great researcher. There’s also the question of: Who will I work with? What scientific questions can I tackle? Will I have the resources and the freedom to pursue something that might take years to work?

You can recruit exceptional individuals, but building an exceptional research team is a different challenge. You need trust, a shared direction, and a culture where people can challenge each other’s ideas. That takes time. So I wouldn’t judge the strategy by the salaries or the announcements. I’d judge it by the research that comes out of it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s importance and scarce frontier researchers, but does not identify safely steering AGI as a motivation for mission-driven researchers.

r002.rationale: It calls the competition understandable, but does not interpret Meta’s offers as an attempt to catch up in AI research.

r003.rationale: The response does not question the meaning of money after AGI.

r004.rationale: It focuses on researcher recruitment and team culture, without discussing how the economy would function after AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, it shows how valuable AI researchers have become. There are relatively few people who have the experience to lead work at the frontier, so it’s understandable that companies are competing very hard for them.

But I think compensation is only part of what attracts and retains great researchers. They also want to know: What’s the scientific ambition? Who will I be working with? Will I have the resources and the freedom to pursue an idea that might take years to work?

You can recruit exceptional individuals, but building a team that consistently makes breakthroughs is a different challenge. That takes trust, a strong research culture, and time. So I’d judge the strategy by the science it produces over the next few years, rather than the size of the offers.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research ambition and resources, but does not mention steering AGI safely as a motivation.

r002.rationale: It calls competition for scarce researchers understandable, but does not frame Meta’s offers as an attempt to catch up in AI research.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss money or compensation in a world after AGI.

r004.rationale: It focuses on research culture and evaluating scientific output, without discussing how an economy might function after AGI.
